newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS - Fresh assault takes S.Africa rand to new low.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Fresh assault takes S.Africa rand to new low.

text.p: The South African rand received a fresh mauling on the foreign exchange markets on Tuesday, hitting a new record low of 4.6910 against the dollar.

The central Reserve Bank stepped in to try and stop the rot, offering dollars aggressively into a tense market, but the currency remained weak and dealers predicted it could test the 4.70 level later in the day.
The currency woes took their toll on other South African markets with long bond yields kicking up to the highest level since June at just under 16 percent.
Shares on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange shed more than one percent of their value by midday as investors, already unsettled by Wall Street's slide, baled out fearing further rand losses.

Dave Mohr, chief economist at the country's biggest life assurance group Old Mutual, said investors had little appetite for South African assets at present with balance of payments difficulties and low reserves dominating sentiment.
"We have the combination of a weak current account position coupled with a weak capital account, causing a fall in foreign exchange reserves which were almost non-existent to start with," he said.

Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals is tackling the current account deficit head on, hoping that high interest rates and a weak currency will close the gap by limiting domestic expenditure and boosting exports.
But Mohr said there could be no overnight turnaround.
"There are long lags involved in the process and it looks like it is early days in the adjustment process," he said.

Stals said on Monday he expected the balance of payments to stabilise and start improving, but the current account deficit was likely to remain around 12 billion rand ($2.55 billion) in 1996, little changed from 1995's 12.7 billion rand.

The rand has lost over 28 percent of its value against the dollar since mid-February when the run on the currency first started on ill-founded rumours about President Nelson Mandela's health and talk of an imminent scrapping of exchange controls.

The government has pledged its commitment to the eventual lifting of rand controls but the lack of a timetable has frustrated investors and encouraged speculators to sell the rand short, anticipating an outflow of funds when controls go.
Stals and Finance Minister Trevor Manuel argue controls cannot be scrapped while foreign reserves remain at current low levels, equivalent to only around four weeks import cover.
Critics counter that as long as restrictions on capital movement remain, the rand will be a target for speculators.

"There is no chance the rand can be a stable or even balanced currency until foreign exchange controls are abolished. I can't see the floor before then," said Peter Cronshaw, chief executive of leading investment company Genbel.
Standard Bank's economics division argued that abolition of controls on residents would give a clear signal of confidence to nervous markets.
In a report published last week, it called on the government to make use of a standby facility from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to beef up its financial resources and then scrap controls.
South Africa could draw up to 100 percent of its IMF quota, or some $2 billion, effectively doubling its existing foreign reserves, the bank's economics division said.

The IMF has applauded South Africa's economic and fiscal policies and made clear its readiness to lend support. But the authorities have so far rejected the idea of IMF funding which would see the Washington institution "policing" domestic policy.
